encoding_log.content:
Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

Images of the nebula tend to leave a strong impression, even on people who don't usually pay much attention to astronomy. The colors and shapes seem almost too vivid to be real, though they're exactly what the telescope captures. It's the kind of sight that makes clear why so many people find deep-sky objects captivating.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

Images of the nebula tend to leave a strong impression, even on people who don't usually pay much attention to astronomy. The colors and shapes seem almost too vivid to be real, though they're exactly what the telescope captures. It's the kind of sight that makes clear why so many people find deep-sky objects captivating.

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

Images of the nebula tend to leave a strong impression, even on people who don't usually pay much attention to astronomy. It's the kind of sight that makes clear why so many people find deep-sky objects captivating.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

Images of the nebula tend to leave a strong impression, even on people who don't usually pay much attention to astronomy. Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. It's the kind of sight that makes clear why so many people find deep-sky objects captivating.

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

Images of the nebula tend to leave a strong impression, even on people who don't usually pay much attention to astronomy. The colors and shapes seem almost too vivid to be real, though they're exactly what the telescope captures. It's the kind of sight that makes clear why so many people find deep-sky objects captivating.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

Images of the nebula tend to leave a strong impression, even on people who don't usually pay much attention to astronomy. The colors and shapes seem almost too vivid to be real, though they're exactly what the telescope captures. It's the kind of sight that makes clear why so many people find deep-sky objects captivating.

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

Images of the nebula tend to leave a strong impression, even on people who don't usually pay much attention to astronomy. Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

Images of the nebula tend to leave a strong impression, even on people who don't usually pay much attention to astronomy. The colors and shapes seem almost too vivid to be real, though they're exactly what the telescope captures. It's the kind of sight that makes clear why so many people find deep-sky objects captivating.

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

encoding_log.content:
Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

Images of the nebula tend to leave a strong impression, even on people who don't usually pay much attention to astronomy. The colors and shapes seem almost too vivid to be real, though they're exactly what the telescope captures. It's the kind of sight that makes clear why so many people find deep-sky objects captivating.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

Images of the nebula tend to leave a strong impression, even on people who don't usually pay much attention to astronomy. The colors and shapes seem almost too vivid to be real, though they're exactly what the telescope captures. It's the kind of sight that makes clear why so many people find deep-sky objects captivating.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

Images of the nebula tend to leave a strong impression, even on people who don't usually pay much attention to astronomy. The colors and shapes seem almost too vivid to be real, though they're exactly what the telescope captures. It's the kind of sight that makes clear why so many people find deep-sky objects captivating.

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

Images of the nebula tend to leave a strong impression, even on people who don't usually pay much attention to astronomy. The colors and shapes seem almost too vivid to be real, though they're exactly what the telescope captures. It's the kind of sight that makes clear why so many people find deep-sky objects captivating.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

Images of the nebula tend to leave a strong impression, even on people who don't usually pay much attention to astronomy. The colors and shapes seem almost too vivid to be real, though they're exactly what the telescope captures. It's the kind of sight that makes clear why so many people find deep-sky objects captivating.

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. Images of the nebula tend to leave a strong impression, even on people who don't usually pay much attention to astronomy. It's the kind of sight that makes clear why so many people find deep-sky objects captivating.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

Images of the nebula tend to leave a strong impression, even on people who don't usually pay much attention to astronomy. The colors and shapes seem almost too vivid to be real, though they're exactly what the telescope captures. It's the kind of sight that makes clear why so many people find deep-sky objects captivating.

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

Images of the nebula tend to leave a strong impression, even on people who don't usually pay much attention to astronomy. The colors and shapes seem almost too vivid to be real, though they're exactly what the telescope captures. It's the kind of sight that makes clear why so many people find deep-sky objects captivating.

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

Images of the nebula tend to leave a strong impression, even on people who don't usually pay much attention to astronomy. The colors and shapes seem almost too vivid to be real, though they're exactly what the telescope captures. It's the kind of sight that makes clear why so many people find deep-sky objects captivating.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

Images of the nebula tend to leave a strong impression, even on people who don't usually pay much attention to astronomy. The colors and shapes seem almost too vivid to be real, though they're exactly what the telescope captures. It's the kind of sight that makes clear why so many people find deep-sky objects captivating.

encoding_log.content:
Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around them until the whole cloud, the whole nebula, shines brightly. 

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulling the gas together until it ignites.

They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope specifically takes in red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around them until the whole cloud, the whole nebula, shines brightly. 

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulling the gas together until it ignites.

They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope specifically takes in red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around them until the whole cloud, the whole nebula, shines brightly. 

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulling the gas together until it ignites.

They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope specifically takes in red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around them until the whole cloud, the whole nebula, shines brightly. 

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulling the gas together until it ignites.

They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope specifically takes in red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around them until the whole cloud, the whole nebula, shines brightly. 

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulling the gas together until it ignites.

They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope specifically takes in red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around them until the whole cloud, the whole nebula, shines brightly. 

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulling the gas together until it ignites.

They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope specifically takes in red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely.

options.2: How gas clouds ignite into new stars
options.3: How gravitational waves ripple through a region of space
options.4: How black hole emissions change

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the Pictor Nebula? Select all that apply.

options.3: The remains of a dying star that is studied to understand how new stars form
options.4: The remains of a dying star that is studied to understand gravitational waves

options.2: A globular pulsar — a cloud of gas lit by its own embedded young stars
options.3: A globular pulsar — the collapsed core of an exploded massive star
options.4: An emission nebula — two stars in a close gravitational orbit

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go.

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around them until the whole cloud, the whole nebula, shines brightly. 

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulling the gas together until it ignites.

They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope specifically takes in red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around them until the whole cloud, the whole nebula, shines brightly. 

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulling the gas together until it ignites.

They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope specifically takes in red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around them until the whole cloud, the whole nebula, shines brightly. 

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulling the gas together until it ignites.

They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope specifically takes in red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around them until the whole cloud, the whole nebula, shines brightly. 

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulling the gas together until it ignites.

They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope specifically takes in red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around them until the whole cloud, the whole nebula, shines brightly. 

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulling the gas together until it ignites.

They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope specifically takes in red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely.

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around them until the whole cloud, the whole nebula, shines brightly. 

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulling the gas together until it ignites.

They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope specifically takes in red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around them until the whole cloud, the whole nebula, shines brightly. 

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulling the gas together until it ignites.

They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope specifically takes in red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely.

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around them until the whole cloud, the whole nebula, shines brightly.

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around them until the whole cloud, the whole nebula, shines brightly. 

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulling the gas together until it ignites.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around them until the whole cloud, the whole nebula, shines brightly. 

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulling the gas together until it ignites.

They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope specifically takes in red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around them until the whole cloud, the whole nebula, shines brightly. 

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulling the gas together until it ignites.

They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope specifically takes in red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around them until the whole cloud, the whole nebula, shines brightly. 

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulling the gas together until it ignites.

They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope specifically takes in red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely.

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around them until the whole cloud, the whole nebula, shines brightly. 

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulling the gas together until it ignites.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around them until the whole cloud, the whole nebula, shines brightly. 

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulling the gas together until it ignites.

They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope specifically takes in red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulls the gas together, making the cloud hotter and denser, hotter and denser, until eventually the star ignites! 

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope is tuned specifically to red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely. At other wavelengths the glow fades almost entirely, so an optical telescope tuned to red light is essential for seeing the nebula's full extent.

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. At other wavelengths the glow fades almost entirely, so an optical telescope tuned to red light is essential for seeing the nebula's full extent.

encoding_log.content:
Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulls the gas together, making the cloud hotter and denser, hotter and denser, until eventually the star ignites! 

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulls the gas together, making the cloud hotter and denser, hotter and denser, until eventually the star ignites! 

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope is tuned specifically to red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely. At other wavelengths the glow fades almost entirely, so an optical telescope tuned to red light is essential for seeing the nebula's full extent.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulls the gas together, making the cloud hotter and denser, hotter and denser, until eventually the star ignites! 

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope is tuned specifically to red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely. At other wavelengths the glow fades almost entirely, so an optical telescope tuned to red light is essential for seeing the nebula's full extent.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulls the gas together, making the cloud hotter and denser, hotter and denser, until eventually the star ignites! 

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope is tuned specifically to red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely. At other wavelengths the glow fades almost entirely, so an optical telescope tuned to red light is essential for seeing the nebula's full extent.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulls the gas together, making the cloud hotter and denser, hotter and denser, until eventually the star ignites! 

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope is tuned specifically to red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely. At other wavelengths the glow fades almost entirely, so an optical telescope tuned to red light is essential for seeing the nebula's full extent.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulls the gas together, making the cloud hotter and denser, hotter and denser, until eventually the star ignites! 

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope is tuned specifically to red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely. At other wavelengths the glow fades almost entirely, so an optical telescope tuned to red light is essential for seeing the nebula's full extent.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulls the gas together, making the cloud hotter and denser, hotter and denser, until eventually the star ignites! 

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope is tuned specifically to red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely. At other wavelengths the glow fades almost entirely, so an optical telescope tuned to red light is essential for seeing the nebula's full extent.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulls the gas together, making the cloud hotter and denser, hotter and denser, until eventually the star ignites! 

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope is tuned specifically to red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely. At other wavelengths the glow fades almost entirely, so an optical telescope tuned to red light is essential for seeing the nebula's full extent.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulls the gas together, making the cloud hotter and denser, hotter and denser, until eventually the star ignites! 

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope is tuned specifically to red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely. At other wavelengths the glow fades almost entirely, so an optical telescope tuned to red light is essential for seeing the nebula's full extent.

encoding_log.content:
Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulls the gas together, making the cloud hotter and denser, hotter and denser, until eventually the star ignites! 

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope is tuned specifically to red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely. At other wavelengths the glow fades almost entirely, so an optical telescope tuned to red light is essential for seeing the nebula's full extent.

encoding_log.content:
Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulls the gas together, making the cloud hotter and denser, hotter and denser, until eventually the star ignites! 

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope is tuned specifically to red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely. At other wavelengths the glow fades almost entirely, so an optical telescope tuned to red light is essential for seeing the nebula's full extent.

encoding_log.content:
Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulls the gas together, making the cloud hotter and denser, hotter and denser, until eventually the star ignites! 

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope is tuned specifically to red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely. At other wavelengths the glow fades almost entirely, so an optical telescope tuned to red light is essential for seeing the nebula's full extent.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulls the gas together, making the cloud hotter and denser, hotter and denser, until eventually the star ignites! 

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope is tuned specifically to red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely. At other wavelengths the glow fades almost entirely, so an optical telescope tuned to red light is essential for seeing the nebula's full extent.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulls the gas together, making the cloud hotter and denser, hotter and denser, until eventually the star ignites! 

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope is tuned specifically to red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely. At other wavelengths the glow fades almost entirely, so an optical telescope tuned to red light is essential for seeing the nebula's full extent.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulls the gas together, making the cloud hotter and denser, hotter and denser, until eventually the star ignites! 

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope is tuned specifically to red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely. At other wavelengths the glow fades almost entirely, so an optical telescope tuned to red light is essential for seeing the nebula's full extent.

encoding_log.content:
Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulls the gas together, making the cloud hotter and denser, hotter and denser, until eventually the star ignites! 

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope is tuned specifically to red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely. At other wavelengths the glow fades almost entirely, so an optical telescope tuned to red light is essential for seeing the nebula's full extent.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulls the gas together, making the cloud hotter and denser, hotter and denser, until eventually the star ignites! 

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope is tuned specifically to red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely. At other wavelengths the glow fades almost entirely, so an optical telescope tuned to red light is essential for seeing the nebula's full extent.

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulls the gas together, making the cloud hotter and denser, hotter and denser, until eventually the star ignites! 

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope is tuned specifically to red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely. At other wavelengths the glow fades almost entirely, so an optical telescope tuned to red light is essential for seeing the nebula's full extent.

encoding_log.content:
Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulls the gas together, making the cloud hotter and denser, hotter and denser, until eventually the star ignites! 

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope is tuned specifically to red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely. At other wavelengths the glow fades almost entirely, so an optical telescope tuned to red light is essential for seeing the nebula's full extent.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulls the gas together, making the cloud hotter and denser, hotter and denser, until eventually the star ignites! 

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope is tuned specifically to red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely. At other wavelengths the glow fades almost entirely, so an optical telescope tuned to red light is essential for seeing the nebula's full extent.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulls the gas together, making the cloud hotter and denser, hotter and denser, until eventually the star ignites! 

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope is tuned specifically to red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely. At other wavelengths the glow fades almost entirely, so an optical telescope tuned to red light is essential for seeing the nebula's full extent.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulls the gas together, making the cloud hotter and denser, hotter and denser, until eventually the star ignites! 

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope is tuned specifically to red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely. At other wavelengths the glow fades almost entirely, so an optical telescope tuned to red light is essential for seeing the nebula's full extent.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulls the gas together, making the cloud hotter and denser, hotter and denser, until eventually the star ignites! 

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope is tuned specifically to red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely. At other wavelengths the glow fades almost entirely, so an optical telescope tuned to red light is essential for seeing the nebula's full extent.

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulls the gas together, making the cloud hotter and denser, hotter and denser, until eventually the star ignites! 

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope is tuned specifically to red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely. At other wavelengths the glow fades almost entirely, so an optical telescope tuned to red light is essential for seeing the nebula's full extent.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulls the gas together, making the cloud hotter and denser, hotter and denser, until eventually the star ignites! 

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope is tuned specifically to red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely. At other wavelengths the glow fades almost entirely, so an optical telescope tuned to red light is essential for seeing the nebula's full extent.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. Four thousand light-years is actually close, as nebulae go. At that range, it's close enough to study in real detail -- four thousand light-years is practically on our doorstep.

The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Those embedded stars heat the gas cloud around  them until the whole cloud, the entire nebula, shines brightly. Because the stars inside the nebula emit their own light, the Pictor nebula is an emission nebula.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. That's how new stars form there — gravity slowly pulls the gas together, making the cloud hotter and denser, hotter and denser, until eventually the star ignites! 

Scientists observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light. That optical telescope is tuned specifically to red light, the frequency at which the nebula's gases shine most intensely. At other wavelengths the glow fades almost entirely, so an optical telescope tuned to red light is essential for seeing the nebula's full extent.

encoding_log.content:
Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

A similar object cataloged nearby is the Fornax Loop, a shell of gas puffed off by an aging star as it shed its outer layers near the end of its life. Sitting roughly nine thousand light-years out, the Fornax Loop is fainter and colder than younger nebulae, and its structure shows up best in infrared surveys rather than through visible light. Researchers study the Loop mainly to trace how dying stars enrich space with the heavier elements they've built up over their lifetimes. Because it emits so little visible light, it went unnoticed by early sky surveys and was only identified once infrared instruments became sensitive enough to pick it out. Spectroscopic analysis shows elevated carbon and nitrogen relative to hydrogen, consistent with material dredged up from the star's core in its final years. The shell is expanding outward at roughly twelve kilometers per second, slow enough that it should fully disperse within about ten thousand years.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

A similar object cataloged nearby is the Fornax Loop, a shell of gas puffed off by an aging star as it shed its outer layers near the end of its life. Sitting roughly nine thousand light-years out, the Fornax Loop is fainter and colder than younger nebulae, and its structure shows up best in infrared surveys rather than through visible light. Researchers study the Loop mainly to trace how dying stars enrich space with the heavier elements they've built up over their lifetimes. Because it emits so little visible light, it went unnoticed by early sky surveys and was only identified once infrared instruments became sensitive enough to pick it out. Spectroscopic analysis shows elevated carbon and nitrogen relative to hydrogen, consistent with material dredged up from the star's core in its final years. The shell is expanding outward at roughly twelve kilometers per second, slow enough that it should fully disperse within about ten thousand years.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

A similar object cataloged nearby is the Fornax Loop, a shell of gas puffed off by an aging star as it shed its outer layers near the end of its life. Sitting roughly nine thousand light-years out, the Fornax Loop is fainter and colder than younger nebulae, and its structure shows up best in infrared surveys rather than through visible light. Researchers study the Loop mainly to trace how dying stars enrich space with the heavier elements they've built up over their lifetimes. Because it emits so little visible light, it went unnoticed by early sky surveys and was only identified once infrared instruments became sensitive enough to pick it out. Spectroscopic analysis shows elevated carbon and nitrogen relative to hydrogen, consistent with material dredged up from the star's core in its final years. The shell is expanding outward at roughly twelve kilometers per second, slow enough that it should fully disperse within about ten thousand years.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

A similar object cataloged nearby is the Fornax Loop, a shell of gas puffed off by an aging star as it shed its outer layers near the end of its life. Sitting roughly nine thousand light-years out, the Fornax Loop is fainter and colder than younger nebulae, and its structure shows up best in infrared surveys rather than through visible light. Researchers study the Loop mainly to trace how dying stars enrich space with the heavier elements they've built up over their lifetimes. Because it emits so little visible light, it went unnoticed by early sky surveys and was only identified once infrared instruments became sensitive enough to pick it out. Spectroscopic analysis shows elevated carbon and nitrogen relative to hydrogen, consistent with material dredged up from the star's core in its final years. The shell is expanding outward at roughly twelve kilometers per second, slow enough that it should fully disperse within about ten thousand years.

Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

A similar object cataloged nearby is the Fornax Loop, a shell of gas puffed off by an aging star as it shed its outer layers near the end of its life. Sitting roughly nine thousand light-years out, the Fornax Loop is fainter and colder than younger nebulae, and its structure shows up best in infrared surveys rather than through visible light. Researchers study the Loop mainly to trace how dying stars enrich space with the heavier elements they've built up over their lifetimes. Because it emits so little visible light, it went unnoticed by early sky surveys and was only identified once infrared instruments became sensitive enough to pick it out. Spectroscopic analysis shows elevated carbon and nitrogen relative to hydrogen, consistent with material dredged up from the star's core in its final years. The shell is expanding outward at roughly twelve kilometers per second, slow enough that it should fully disperse within about ten thousand years.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

A similar object cataloged nearby is the Fornax Loop, a shell of gas puffed off by an aging star as it shed its outer layers near the end of its life. Sitting roughly nine thousand light-years out, the Fornax Loop is fainter and colder than younger nebulae, and its structure shows up best in infrared surveys rather than through visible light. Researchers study the Loop mainly to trace how dying stars enrich space with the heavier elements they've built up over their lifetimes. Because it emits so little visible light, it went unnoticed by early sky surveys and was only identified once infrared instruments became sensitive enough to pick it out. Spectroscopic analysis shows elevated carbon and nitrogen relative to hydrogen, consistent with material dredged up from the star's core in its final years. The shell is expanding outward at roughly twelve kilometers per second, slow enough that it should fully disperse within about ten thousand years.

They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

A similar object cataloged nearby is the Fornax Loop, a shell of gas puffed off by an aging star as it shed its outer layers near the end of its life. Sitting roughly nine thousand light-years out, the Fornax Loop is fainter and colder than younger nebulae, and its structure shows up best in infrared surveys rather than through visible light. Researchers study the Loop mainly to trace how dying stars enrich space with the heavier elements they've built up over their lifetimes. Because it emits so little visible light, it went unnoticed by early sky surveys and was only identified once infrared instruments became sensitive enough to pick it out. Spectroscopic analysis shows elevated carbon and nitrogen relative to hydrogen, consistent with material dredged up from the star's core in its final years. The shell is expanding outward at roughly twelve kilometers per second, slow enough that it should fully disperse within about ten thousand years.

encoding_log.content:
Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

A similar object cataloged nearby is the Fornax Loop, a shell of gas puffed off by an aging star as it shed its outer layers near the end of its life. Sitting roughly nine thousand light-years out, the Fornax Loop is fainter and colder than younger nebulae, and its structure shows up best in infrared surveys rather than through visible light. Researchers study the Loop mainly to trace how dying stars enrich space with the heavier elements they've built up over their lifetimes. Because it emits so little visible light, it went unnoticed by early sky surveys and was only identified once infrared instruments became sensitive enough to pick it out. Spectroscopic analysis shows elevated carbon and nitrogen relative to hydrogen, consistent with material dredged up from the star's core in its final years. The shell is expanding outward at roughly twelve kilometers per second, slow enough that it should fully disperse within about ten thousand years.

Topic: astronomy

About four thousand light-years away from Earth sits the Pictor Nebula. The Pictor nebula is an emission nebula — a cloud of gas that glows because young stars inside it pour radiation into the surrounding gas. Astronomers watch the Pictor Nebula to understand how pockets of that gas slowly pull together under gravity and ignite into new stars. They observe this process with an optical telescope, tuned to red light.

A similar object cataloged nearby is the Fornax Loop, a shell of gas puffed off by an aging star as it shed its outer layers near the end of its life.
